IoT data engineering

Construction Site Safety Monitoring

A wearable system that tracks how construction workers move and flags the moments that matter for safety. Four Arduino Nesso N1 devices with a BMI270 accelerometer and gyroscope stream readings at 2 Hz over Bluetooth Low Energy to a Python collector.

  1. WearableBMI270, 2 Hz
  2. BLE stream
  3. Python collector
  4. Threshold rules
  5. SQLite
  6. Flask dashboardon Render
  • Validated readings with threshold-based rules and sorted them into Fall From Height, Slip-Trip-Fall and Near Miss events.
  • Built a Flask dashboard to search by worker, filter by date, time and event type, and analyse incident trends.
  • Deployed it on Render so past incidents can be reviewed remotely.
The problemFalls, slips and trips on site can cause serious injury or death, and early detection and monitoring are hard on large sites.
Our solutionMonitor workers in real time with wearable sensors, classify safety events automatically, and store the data for historical analysis.
Who uses itSite supervisors and safety officers, through an easy-to-use dashboard for monitoring and reporting.
What the system recordedSelect an event type to find it on the trace

2,025 events in total, recorded while testing with 4 workers.

The trace illustrates the kind of signal the rules sort into events. The counts are from testing.

Built with
Design thinking, team of four

Adjustable Wheelchair Prototype

A group project to make a wheelchair more comfortable for the person using it. We built a working LEGO prototype with a backrest that a DC motor raises and lowers, controlled by two buttons through an Arduino. My part was the visual prototype, the storyboard and the value-effort map.

Our user finds her wheelchair uncomfortable because it cannot be adjusted. It affects her daily life and makes her feel she is not in control of it.

How might we design a suitable device that can benefit wheelchair users to make it more comfortable for them?

If a wheelchair feels like part of the user rather than a device, they can use it regularly and live almost as comfortably as people without disabilities.

Each of us sketched ideas in a Crazy 8s round, then I placed them on a value-effort map. The adjustable backrest landed in the high value, low effort corner, so we built it first.

FeatureProduct AProduct BOur idea
Seat cushionYesYesYes
Adjustable backrestYesYesYes
Adjustable leg restNoYesYes
For personal useYesNoYes

Our competitor study found one chair without an adjustable leg rest and one made only for hospitals, so we aimed at personal use.

We used the LEGO Prototyping Kit, with three parts working together.

  • MechanicalA DC motor moves the adjustable backrest, and LEGO parts form the frame.
  • ElectronicWe wired the DC motor in Tinkercad first to check the circuit worked.
  • ProgrammingAn Arduino drives the motor back and forth using two buttons.

Challenges

  • The first wheelchair was too small to present as a prototype, so we rebuilt it from scratch.
  • We had no clear vision until the Crazy 8s round and the decision matrix, which left little time. We worked through it.

Fixes

  • Testing the circuit showed the backrest would not rise past a certain angle, so we added a guard to stop it going back so far.
  • The code went through many iterations, because the problem was sometimes the wiring rather than the code.

Design enhancements

  • Improve the leg guard design.
  • Reposition the motor and improve its efficiency, which could remove the need for the back guard.

Safety improvements

  • The backrest currently leans too far forward.
  • Add a stopper to limit unsafe movement.
Built with
IoT, Arduino and Raspberry Pi

Touchless Smart Lighting System

A light you never have to touch. An ultrasonic sensor notices when someone is in the room and switches the LED on, and off again when the readings stop changing. A gesture sensor dims the light when I wave down and brings it back when I wave up. An Arduino Uno reads both sensors every half second and sends the data over serial to a Raspberry Pi, which stores it in MariaDB and shows it on a Flask dashboard in real time.

Shared switchesEveryone touches them, so bacteria spread in classrooms and offices.
Wear and tearConstant use wears switches out over time.
Forgotten lightsLights left on in empty rooms waste energy.
  1. Gesture and ultrasonic sensors
  2. Arduino Unoreads every 0.5 s
  3. Serial link
  4. Raspberry PiPython on Thonny
  5. MariaDB
  6. Flask dashboardreal-time data

Live Thonny output

How it works

Steady distance readings mean an empty room, so the LED turns off. Changing readings mean movement, so it turns on. A downward swipe dims the light and an upward swipe resets the brightness, with no touching.

Data collected

Distance, LED status, gesture and brightness, logged to MariaDB every 0.5 seconds and shown on the Flask dashboard in real time.

Try it: a simulation of my test cases

Led_status: ON | Gesture: None | Brightness: 255

The row mirrors the columns I store in MariaDB. Brightness is 255 normally, 30 when dimmed and 0 when the LED is off, as in my test cases.

Test results: 3 of 3 passed

ConditionLEDBrightnessResult
Person detected, wave downON30Pass
No person detectedOFF0Pass
Person detected, no gestureON255Pass

A wiring problem

The gesture sensor kept failing over I2C until I realised the wires were faulty. After I changed them, it worked normally.

What I learned

A Flask server has to be handled carefully while the database is being updated. Reliable serial communication between the Arduino and Raspberry Pi was my biggest win.

What I would add next

A short delay before the light switches off, so it does not flicker if I step away for a moment, and a buzzer that sounds when nobody is detected.

Built with
Cloud computing, EG2A16 Cloud Computing Development

Musical Instrument Shop on AWS

The brief was to build a cost-effective, reliable, efficient and secure cloud application for an e-commerce business, within a $50 budget and a fixed timeframe. It had to include a web server, a VPC, a database and object storage, and its home page had to show nine products, with the product details in the database and the images in object storage. I built a shop selling musical instruments, then improved it across six areas: security, reliability, cost, operations, performance and sustainability.

How the shop works

A visitor opens the shop at the web server's public IP address and sees nine instruments: drums, electric guitar, flute, guitar, harp, piano, tabla, trumpet and violin, each with an image, price and description. The page is built by a Flask application that runs on an EC2 instance behind nginx. Each time the page loads, the app connects to an RDS MySQL database, reads the nine product records from the products table and fills them into an HTML template. The browser then loads the nine images from the S3 bucket using the URLs written into the page. Text lives in the database and pictures in object storage, and the app joins them on every page load.

The architecture. Select a part to read more.

VPC 10.0.0.0/16

A visitor opens the shop in a browser, using the web server's fixed public address. The home page lists nine products with a photo, name, price and description.

Network

A VPC called 252662H-vpc with four subnets over two availability zones: two public (10.0.0.0/20 and 10.0.16.0/20) and two private (10.0.128.0/20 and 10.0.144.0/20), plus an internet gateway and route tables.

Compute and database

The EC2 web server sits in a public subnet and has a fixed Elastic IP. The encrypted RDS MySQL database (20 GB) sits in the private subnets, is not publicly accessible, and uses a subnet group that spans both zones.

Storage

The S3 bucket 252662h-bucket holds the nine product images. A second bucket, 252662h-bucket-logs, receives its access logs and is not public.

The finished shop

Six improvements after the first working version

  • Cut the SSH attack surface from the whole IPv4 address space to my own IP address only.
  • Made the database unreachable from the public internet. Only the application tier can connect to it, on the MySQL port.
  • Wrote a bucket policy so visitors can read the product images without signing in, because the page links to them by URL. The policy grants only read access, so nobody can upload, change, delete or list the bucket's contents.
  • The shop still showed all nine products afterwards, so the change cost no functionality.
1 to 7 daysdatabase backup recovery window
Fixed IPan Elastic IP that can be remapped to a replacement server
  • Raised the recovery window from one day to seven, so a data problem found up to a week later can still be traced and recovered.
  • Turned on deletion protection so the instances cannot be destroyed by accident.
  • Turned on bucket versioning, so a deleted product image is no longer lost for good and earlier versions can be restored.
  • Attached an Elastic IP, a static address that can be moved to a new instance within seconds if one fails. Before, a failure would have given a new, unpredictable address and broken every link.

Versioning improves reliability, but it keeps every overwritten or deleted image forever, so storage charges keep growing. I added a lifecycle rule to the bucket that permanently deletes non-current object versions after 30 days and removes incomplete multipart uploads after 7 days.

The storage used by old image versions is now capped. Without the rule, every re-upload would add to the bill for good. The whole project finished inside the $50 budget.

If a product image stopped showing, I would only find out when someone noticed the page looked wrong, with no way to tell whether the object was missing, misnamed or blocked by permissions. I turned on server access logging, so every request to the bucket is recorded with its object key and response code. A failure can now be found in the log instead of by guessing.

The nine images were being served with no Cache-Control header, so a browser had no instruction on how long to reuse a downloaded copy and fetched every image again on each page load. I set public, max-age=31536000 on all nine objects using the AWS CLI in CloudShell, because the S3 console in this environment has no option to edit that metadata.

Images are now cached by the browser for up to a year. A first visit downloads the nine images as before, but each returning visitor saves nine round trips to S3, which means faster pages and fewer S3 requests and less data transfer.

Checking the page in the browser's network panel showed that piano.jpg was 1,067 kB of a 1.3 MB page, about 80% of everything transferred. It was stored at 4000 by 3000 pixels but displayed only 400 pixels wide. I re-encoded it to 800 pixels wide at quality 80 with ImageMagick in CloudShell and re-uploaded it, keeping its Content-Type and Cache-Control settings.

-81%data per page load, from 1.3 MB to 245 kB
-95%size of the biggest image, the piano
2.65 to 1.30 spage load time, as measured in my report

The original held roughly 100 times more pixels than the page needs, so there is no visible loss of quality. Less data means less network energy and less work for each visitor's device on every page view.

Built with
Machine learning

Parkinson's Disease Classification

A supervised classification project in Python. Using voice measurements recorded from 195 samples, I trained a decision tree and a random forest to predict whether a sample is from a person with Parkinson's disease, tuned both, and compared them fairly on data they had never seen. It was a coursework exercise on a small public dataset, not a medical tool.

195voice samples, each with 22 measurements such as jitter, shimmer and pitch
147 / 48Parkinson's against not: 75% to 25%, an imbalanced target
190samples kept after removing 7 rows with missing values
  • Checked the data first: 7 missing values (about 3.6% of rows) and no duplicates.
  • Dropped name, a unique ID with no predictive value, and DCAT, a column of 26 near-random categories with no clear meaning.
  • Dropped the 7 incomplete rows rather than filling them in. At this size, filling could distort the spread of the data and losing 7 rows costs very little.
  • Did not scale features, because trees split on each feature on its own, so differences in scale do not matter.
  • Split the data 70/30 with a stratified split (seed 42), giving 133 training and 57 test rows. Stratifying keeps the Parkinson's and not-Parkinson's mix the same in both: the test set has 43 and 14.

Baseline. An unrestricted tree grew to 25 nodes and 5 levels and scored 100% on the training data but only 82.5% on the test data. That gap is overfitting: it had memorised the training set. It also caught only 36% of the not-Parkinson's samples.

Tuning. I used GridSearchCV to search tree depth, how many features each split can see, the minimum samples per leaf (1, 2, 4, 8) and the split criterion (gini or entropy). The best tree used entropy, depth 3 and at least 4 samples per leaf, so it shrank to 11 nodes.

86.0%test accuracy, up from 82.5%
0.64not-Parkinson's recall, up from 0.36

Training accuracy fell from 100% to 95.5%, which is what a model that generalises better looks like.

A single tree is easy to explain, because any prediction can be traced split by split, but it stays sensitive to the exact training data. That is why I moved to an ensemble next.

A random forest averages many trees trained on random slices of the data and features, so their individual mistakes tend to cancel. To choose the number of trees, I used out-of-bag error, which tests each tree on the samples it never saw, with no separate validation set needed.

Out-of-bag error by number of trees. Lower is better.

The error bottomed out at 100 trees, then stayed flat to 400. I then ran GridSearchCV over trees, depth, leaf size and class weights. It chose 200 trees, with the same test score as the 100-tree forest. Two different methods agreeing is a good sign the result is stable.

87.7%test accuracy, the best of the three models
0.98Parkinson's recall: it caught 42 of the 43 real cases

Select a model to see its test-set scores

Why I chose the random forest

It had the best test accuracy (87.7% against 86.0%) and the strongest recall on Parkinson's cases (0.98 against 0.93). In a screening setting, missing a real case costs more than a false alarm, so that matters most.

What it gave up

It caught fewer of the not-Parkinson's samples than the tuned tree (0.57 against 0.64), and it is harder to explain and slower to train. The tree's strength is that you can trace every prediction.

A caveat I would put on any of these numbers: the test set has only 57 rows and just 14 of them are not-Parkinson's, so one extra mistake moves a score a lot. The classes are also imbalanced, which is why I looked at recall for each class and not only accuracy.

Built with
Product modelling and prototyping

Keychain microSD Card Holder

The brief: design and 3D print a functional object with at least three CAD features, such as holes, chamfers, fillets, slots, recesses, protruding bosses or polygons, then produce a dimensioned technical drawing and a physical print.

My idea: I take photos, so I always need a microSD card on me. I designed this holder to carry two cards on a keychain attached to my bag, so I do not leave one behind. Select the dots on the photo, or the features beside it.

What went wrong

My first print failed. A floating section formed incorrectly onto the layer beneath it. The cause was that I had not sliced and checked the model first, so the support gap it needed was never generated.

What I learned

3D printers cannot print unsupported "thin air", so slicing and checking supports is a required step before printing. I fixed my workflow, and the next print worked: a holder for two microSD cards, with a keychain hole and an engraved name tag.
